tasks.solution_overview: These terms come from a technical vocabulary in which neighbouring words divide the ground precisely: settled presence against sudden outbreak, prevention against treatment, relief against cure, chance discovery against targeted search. Read the clause that reports what actually happened — when the parasite arrived, when the drug was started, what the therapy achieved — and measure the term against that report. Where the facts belong to the neighbouring term, the writer has chosen by sound rather than by definition.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The ministry described the malaria burden in the highlands as "endemic", noting that the parasite had arrived only that spring and was doubling week on week.**

"Endemic" describes a disease that is constantly present in a population at a fairly steady, expected level, which implies a long settled history in that place. The clause after the comma reports the opposite history: a parasite that reached the highlands months earlier and is still doubling week on week. Sudden arrival plus accelerating growth above any expected baseline is what "epidemic" names.

**Trap:** Endemic reports how permanently a disease sits in a population, not how severe or alarming it currently feels.

A burden that began last spring has no settled baseline to be endemic at, so the label misdescribes it — "epidemic" is the word these facts call for.

**B) Clinicians called the antibiotic course "prophylactic", although it was begun only after the surgical wound had already turned septic.**

A "prophylactic" drug is given before disease appears, precisely so that it never takes hold; the surgical version is the dose administered in the hour before the first incision. Here the timing runs the other way, since the course started once the wound was already infected, which makes the intention treatment rather than prevention. The word for a drug aimed at an infection that has arrived is therapeutic.

Nothing was being prevented by the time this course began, so the description does not hold — the antibiotic was therapeutic, not prophylactic.

**C) The vaccine uses an "attenuated" strain, weakened through repeated passage in culture until it provokes immunity without producing the illness.**

"Attenuated" means reduced in strength while still alive and able to replicate, which is exactly the compromise a live vaccine depends on. The sentence supplies both halves of that definition: repeated passage in culture as the method of weakening, and immunity without illness as the result. A strain that had simply been killed would be inactivated, a different category with different handling.

Weakening that preserves the organism while removing its power to cause disease is the sense the word carries, so the usage is exactly right here.

**D) The unit presented the new therapy as "palliative", reporting that it had cleared the tumour completely in most of the patients treated.**

"Palliative" care eases symptoms and protects comfort without attempting to remove the underlying disease, which is why it is offered when cure is no longer the aim. Clearing a tumour completely is the definition of the opposite intention, and the results clause makes that outcome explicit. Curative is the term for a therapy that eliminates the disease itself.

An outcome that removes the tumour lands well outside what the word claims, so the description fails — such a therapy is curative rather than palliative.

**E) The registry logged the aneurysm as an "incidental" finding, even though the patient had been scanned precisely because of the headaches it was later shown to cause.**

An "incidental" finding turns up by chance while clinicians are looking for something else entirely, which is why it carries no diagnostic credit for the scan that revealed it. This scan was ordered for the very symptom the aneurysm produced, so the discovery was the object of the search rather than a by-product of it. The concession introduced by "even though" quietly reports that mismatch.

The scan went looking for exactly what it found, so the finding cannot be incidental in any useful sense of the word.

tasks.solution_overview: Legal vocabulary is unforgiving because each term names one procedural fact and refuses the neighbouring one: a verdict of not guilty is not a discontinued file, a sentence reduction is not an excuse, and a ruling that may be cited is not one that must be followed. Ask what event or authority each word presupposes, then check whether the sentence actually reports that event. The concessive clauses are where the giveaway usually sits.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The judge treated the defendant's youth and immediate confession as "mitigating", factors that lower the sentence without denying that the offence took place.**

"Mitigating" circumstances reduce the punishment attached to conduct whose wrongfulness is already accepted, which is why they belong to sentencing rather than to the finding of guilt. Youth and an early admission are the standard examples, and the appositive clause states the distinction that matters: the penalty falls, the offence stands. A factor that denied the offence altogether would be a defence, not mitigation.

Reduction in sentence without any challenge to liability is precisely what the term covers, so the wording is used correctly here.

**B) A later profile said the suspect had been "acquitted", though prosecutors had quietly dropped the file two years before any trial began.**

To be "acquitted" is to be found not guilty by a court that has heard the case, so the word presupposes a trial and a verdict. Charges withdrawn before proceedings start produce no verdict at all; the case is discontinued, and the suspect is left neither convicted nor cleared by any tribunal. Journalists often blur the two because the practical effect on the person looks similar.

There was no trial to deliver a verdict, so the word overstates what happened — the prosecution was dropped, not defeated.

**C) The appeal court "remanded" the case, sending it back for the trial judge to make findings on evidence he had never addressed.**

In appellate practice a case is "remanded" when the higher court returns it to the court below for further work rather than deciding the point itself. The sentence describes exactly that manoeuvre, naming both the destination and the task: findings on evidence the trial judge left untouched. Note the contrast with quashing, which ends the matter rather than passing it back.

Returning a case for a lower court to finish the job is the whole meaning of the verb, so the line reads correctly.

**D) Counsel offered the tribunal's ruling as binding "precedent", while conceding that decisions of that body bind no court at all.**

Binding "precedent" is authority a later court is obliged to follow, and that obligation depends entirely on the deciding body's place in the judicial hierarchy. A ruling from a tribunal whose decisions bind nobody can still be cited and may be found convincing, but its force is persuasive only. The concession in the second half removes the very condition the first half claims.

Authority that no court is obliged to follow cannot be binding precedent, so the claim collapses under counsel's own admission — persuasive is as far as it reaches.

**E) The judgment called the award "punitive", explaining that it did no more than restore the sums the claimant had provably lost.**

"Punitive" damages are awarded to punish and deter a defendant, so by definition they exceed the claimant's proven loss. An award that restores exactly what was lost and nothing beyond it is compensatory, the ordinary measure in civil litigation. The explanatory clause states the figure's whole basis and leaves no room for a penal element.

An award confined to proven loss punishes nobody, so the description misfires — compensatory is the right label for this sum.

tasks.solution_overview: Research writing uses a small set of words to grade how much weight a result can bear, and each one carries a claim about the evidence behind it: unsystematic against calibrated, artefactual against replicated, provisional against settled. Read the clause that describes how the observation was made and how often it was repeated, since that is the evidence the adjective is answerable to. When the description reports a stronger or weaker basis than the word allows, the mismatch is the whole question.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The review dismissed the result as "anecdotal", though it rests on eleven years of calibrated photometry from three independent observatories.**

Evidence is "anecdotal" when it consists of scattered, informal reports gathered without design or calibration, which is why it cannot support a general claim. Eleven years of calibrated measurement from three separate observatories is systematic evidence of the strongest routine kind, gathered to a protocol and cross-checked between sites. The concessive "though" flags the collision between the dismissal and the description.

Calibrated long-baseline photometry is the antithesis of a collection of stories, so the dismissal misapplies the word — this evidence is systematic.

**B) The burst was written off as "spurious" after four telescopes on separate continents recorded it at the same instant with matching profiles.**

A "spurious" signal is not real: it originates in the instrument, the software or local interference rather than in the sky. Simultaneous detection by four widely separated telescopes, with profiles that agree, is the standard test that rules such an origin out, since no local artefact reaches four continents at once. A genuine signal may still be unexplained, but unexplained and spurious are not the same verdict.

Independent corroboration at that scale is what establishes a real detection, so calling the burst spurious runs against the very evidence cited for it.

**C) The mass estimate is "tentative", drawn from a single occultation and expected to move once a second timing is obtained.**

"Tentative" marks a figure offered provisionally, with the author signalling in advance that it may be revised. The sentence gives both grounds for that caution: one measurement rather than many, and an explicit expectation that a further timing will shift the value. The word makes a claim about confidence rather than about correctness, which is why it sits comfortably beside a number that may yet turn out to be right.

A single-measurement value the authors expect to revise is exactly what the adjective is for, so the wording stands.

**D) The dust detector flew as "ancillary" instrumentation, supporting the camera rather than driving the measurement the mission was built to make.**

Something "ancillary" is subordinate and supporting, added to help the main effort rather than to define it. The sentence sets up that hierarchy explicitly, with the camera carrying the mission's central measurement and the detector attending on it. The word says nothing about scientific value, only about where an instrument sits in the mission's design.

A supporting role beside a primary instrument is the relationship the word names, so it is well chosen here.

**E) The probe's slow drift is called "anomalous" because it survives after every known force acting on the spacecraft has been modelled and subtracted.**

An "anomalous" measurement departs from what accepted theory predicts, and the label is earned only once the ordinary explanations have been eliminated. That elimination is exactly what the causal clause reports: known forces modelled, subtracted, and the drift still there. Anomalies are interesting precisely because they are residual rather than merely surprising.

A residue that outlives every conventional explanation is the textbook case for the word, so the sentence uses it properly.

tasks.solution_overview: Ecological vocabulary hides precise commitments inside ordinary-looking words: a species that breeds unaided is not merely present, a partnership that benefits one side is not a partnership, and a dispute with long-standing parties on both sides has a name of its own. Take each word back to the condition it asserts, then look for the clause that either supplies that condition or quietly withdraws it. The direction in which the benefit or the evidence flows usually settles the item.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The wall lizard is now "naturalised" along the south coast, breeding unaided in a country it first reached in the 1950s.**

A "naturalised" species is one introduced from elsewhere that now maintains itself without human help, reproducing in the wild generation after generation. The sentence supplies both conditions the term requires: foreign origin, dated to the 1950s, and self-sustaining breeding since. Naturalised is deliberately neutral about harm, which is why a naturalised population need not be an invasive one.

Foreign origin plus unassisted breeding is the whole content of the term, so it is applied correctly here.

**B) The restored marsh is "self-seeding": each spring it regenerates from its own plants, with nothing further sown by the trust.**

"Self-seeding" describes vegetation that renews itself from the seed its own plants shed, without any further sowing. The colon introduces precisely that account: annual regeneration from the site's own stock, and no continuing intervention by the managers. It is a claim about the source of the seed, not about how quickly or thickly the plants return.

Regeneration from the marsh's own seed with no further sowing is exactly the condition named, so the description holds.

**C) Returning lynx to the uplands remains a "vexed" question, pressed for decades by conservation bodies and resisted just as long by hill farmers.**

A "vexed" question is one argued over at length without resolution, with entrenched parties and no settlement in sight; the collocation is a fixed favourite of formal prose. The sentence supplies the two features the phrase implies: opposed camps, and decades of unresolved argument between them. A merely difficult question could be settled by better evidence, whereas a vexed one has resisted that treatment.

Long-running, unresolved dispute between committed opponents is the situation the adjective names, so the phrase fits this sentence exactly.

**D) Recovery of the blanket bog is "incremental", measured in a few millimetres of new moss in a good year.**

"Incremental" change arrives in small successive additions rather than in a single leap, and the word is neutral about whether the total eventually becomes large. Millimetres of moss accumulating annually is that pattern in its purest form, with each year's gain resting on the last. Peat systems are the standard illustration, since their recovery is counted in decades.

Slow accumulation in small regular steps is the sense the adjective carries, so it describes this recovery accurately.

**E) The survey called the association "mutualistic", noting that the mistletoe draws water and minerals from the oak and returns nothing to it.**

A "mutualistic" association benefits both partners, which is what separates it from the other close biological relationships. The clause after the comma describes a one-way transfer: resources move from the oak to the mistletoe, with no return flow of any kind. A relationship in which one organism gains at the host's expense is parasitism.

Benefit running in one direction only is the defining mark of parasitism, so the survey has reached for the wrong term here.

tasks.solution_overview: Field archaeology reports both what survives and how confidently it can be read, and the vocabulary keeps those two things apart: how complete the record is, how independently a date has been checked, how much of an interpretation rests on inference. Match each word against the concrete detail that follows it — the list of surviving features, the second dating method, the single supporting observation. Where description and adjective describe the same state of the evidence, the word is doing its job.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The record of the settlement is "fragmentary": three burnt floors, a scatter of postholes, and nothing at all in between.**

Evidence is "fragmentary" when only disconnected pieces of it survive, leaving gaps that no amount of care can fill. The inventory after the colon is exactly that: a handful of features with acknowledged emptiness between them. The word describes the completeness of the record rather than the quality of the excavation that recovered it.

Isolated survivals separated by blanks are what the adjective names, so it characterises this record precisely.

**B) The radiocarbon range was "corroborated" when ring counts from the roof timbers, measured independently, fell inside it.**

To be "corroborated" is to be supported by separate evidence arrived at by another route, which is stronger than being merely repeated. The sentence supplies that independence twice over: a different method, dendrochronology, and a measurement made separately from the radiocarbon work. Agreement between two unrelated techniques is the classic ground for confidence in a date.

Independent support from a second method is the whole meaning of the verb, so the sentence uses it correctly.

**C) Calling the building a temple is "speculative", resting on its orientation alone, with no inscription, offering or burial to support the reading.**

An interpretation is "speculative" when it runs beyond the evidence available, offered as a possibility rather than a conclusion. Orientation is suggestive but weak on its own, and the sentence lists the three kinds of confirming find that are missing. The word passes judgement on the support for the claim, not on the claim's plausibility.

A reading built on one indirect observation and no confirming finds is speculation by definition, so the label is accurate here.

**D) The excavation was "meticulous", every find plotted to the centimetre and every bucket of soil sieved before it left the trench.**

"Meticulous" work shows extreme attention to small details, carried through consistently rather than in bursts. Centimetre-level recording and the sieving of every bucket are exactly such details, and the repeated "every" reports that the standard held throughout. Slow and thorough are related but weaker: neither insists on this level of precision.

Systematic attention to the smallest detail is the sense the adjective carries, so it describes this fieldwork well.

**E) Her catalogue of the site was "posthumous", assembled by former students from notebooks she had not lived to edit.**

"Posthumous" describes something that happens or appears after the death of the person concerned, most often a publication, an award or a reputation. The relative clause states the fact the word depends on, since the notebooks outlived their author and were prepared by others. It is the appearance of the work, not its writing, that the adjective dates.

A catalogue published after its author's death is the standard case for the word, so this line holds.

tasks.solution_overview: Technical documentation borrows ordinary words and narrows them, so the everyday sense is exactly the trap: discouraged rather than merely old, duplicated on purpose rather than wasteful, privately controlled rather than merely commercial. Take each term back to the specific engineering condition it asserts, then read the clause that reports what the system actually does. Where a word names a quantity, check that the definition offered beside it measures the same thing.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The reference marks the function as "deprecated", recommending it as the preferred choice for all new code.**

To mark something "deprecated" is to discourage its use, usually because a better replacement exists and removal is planned for a later release. The label warns readers away rather than towards, which is why deprecated features keep working while quietly losing support. Recommending a function for all new code is the opposite instruction, and the word for that is preferred or recommended.

A deprecation notice steers new code elsewhere, so the sentence has the guidance exactly back to front.

**B) The flight computer is "redundant" by design: three identical units run the same calculation so that a single failure changes nothing.**

In engineering, "redundant" does not mean wasteful; it means deliberately duplicated so that the loss of one component leaves the function intact. The colon supplies the standard triple-modular arrangement and its purpose, which is tolerance of a single failure.

**Trap:** In engineering prose, redundant means spare capacity held on purpose; the everyday sense of surplus and unwanted points the wrong way.

Deliberate duplication that preserves the function through a failure is exactly what the engineering term means, so the description is sound.

**C) The archive format is described as "proprietary", published as an open specification that anyone may implement without permission or fee.**

A "proprietary" format is controlled by its owner, who decides who may implement it and on what terms, and the specification is often withheld altogether. A published specification that anyone may implement without permission or fee removes both conditions, since nothing is being withheld and no permission is required. Open is the word for a standard released on those terms.

Free and unrestricted implementation is the negation of proprietary control, so the label contradicts the description that follows it.

**D) Engineers blamed the stutter on high "throughput", the delay between a key press and the character appearing on screen.**

"Throughput" measures how much work a system completes in a given period — requests served, frames rendered, bytes written — so it counts volume rather than waiting. The definition supplied in apposition describes something else entirely: the interval between an input and its visible effect, which is latency. The two often trade against each other, and a system can have excellent throughput and dreadful latency at once.

The gloss in this sentence defines latency, so the term chosen names the wrong quantity — high latency is what produces the stutter.

**E) The reporting script is "brittle": it runs perfectly until a column is renamed, and then fails outright with no useful message.**

Code is called "brittle" when it works only under the exact conditions it was written for and breaks completely at the first small departure from them. The colon gives that profile precisely: flawless behaviour until a trivial change to a name, then total failure rather than graceful degradation. Robust code is the contrast, absorbing such changes without collapse.

Perfect behaviour up to a hairline change and outright failure after it is the very pattern the metaphor describes, so the word is apt.

tasks.solution_overview: Administrative language is written to be quoted, so its terms make precise claims about obligation and status: required by law or chosen freely, guiding or enforceable, suspended or abandoned. Test each word against the clause that says who had to do what, and with what consequence for ignoring it. One item turns on tone rather than legal force, so judge that one by the manner of the writing instead.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The final report was "anodyne", phrased so carefully that no councillor, officer or campaign group could take offence at a single line.**

"Anodyne" describes writing so inoffensive that it says nothing anyone could object to, and the word carries a faint note of disappointment at that blandness. The clause after the comma gives the test that matters: careful phrasing designed to leave three separate constituencies with nothing to attack. Diplomatic praises the same restraint, whereas anodyne suggests the price paid for it.

Language shaped to give no one anything to dispute is exactly what the adjective names, so it describes this report well.

**B) The council called the consultation "statutory", explaining that it had chosen to hold one although no legislation required it.**

Something "statutory" is required or created by an Act, which is why statutory consultations have fixed periods and can be challenged if skipped. The explanation attached here withdraws that basis in so many words: the exercise was a choice, and no legislation demanded it. Voluntary or discretionary is the word for a step an authority takes of its own accord.

A consultation held by choice has no statutory foundation to appeal to, so the description fails — this one was discretionary.

**C) Cycle provision in the city grew "piecemeal", a lane added here and a junction redesigned there, with no plan connecting the pieces.**

"Piecemeal" development happens one unconnected piece at a time, without an overall design shaping the sequence. The sentence illustrates the term rather than merely asserting it: individual interventions in scattered places, and an explicit absence of any plan linking them. The word usually implies mild criticism, since piecemeal results tend not to add up.

Isolated additions with nothing coordinating them is precisely what the adverbial sense conveys, so the wording stands.

**D) The authority imposed a "moratorium" on demolition consents, suspending all decisions for two years while a heritage survey was completed.**

A "moratorium" is a temporary and deliberate suspension of an activity, usually declared while some further step is taken. Both elements appear here: a stated two-year pause, and the survey whose completion is the reason for it. A permanent stop would be a ban, and the difference is exactly the expectation that the activity resumes.

A time-limited suspension pending a specific piece of work is the sense the noun carries, so it is used properly in this line.

**E) The published traffic figures were labelled "indicative", although the authority treats them as binding limits and fines operators who exceed them.**

Figures described as "indicative" are offered as a guide to the likely scale of something, explicitly not as commitments that anyone can be held to. Limits enforced by fines are the opposite species of number, since exceeding them carries a defined penalty. Binding or mandatory is the honest label for a threshold with a sanction attached.

A number that triggers a fine when exceeded is doing far more than indicating, so the label understates what these figures are.

tasks.solution_overview: Biological description leans on terms that classify strategy rather than describe a single episode: sociable or solitary, generalist or specialist, hidden by pattern or by hiding place, dependent by necessity or by preference. Read the behavioural evidence in the clause that follows and ask whether it reports a habit or an exception. Where a word names a strategy and the sentence describes the opposite strategy, the specialist sense is the one being tested.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The species is "gregarious" outside the breeding season, feeding in flocks of several thousand along the shelf edge.**

Applied to animals, "gregarious" means habitually living and moving in groups rather than alone, a description of social structure rather than of temperament. Flocks of several thousand at the feeding grounds is that habit at scale, and the seasonal qualifier is a normal refinement, since many species are sociable only part of the year. The human sense of a sociable personality is a separate development of the same word.

Group living as the species' normal condition is what the term reports, so the sentence uses it correctly.

**B) The shark is called an "opportunistic" feeder, taking one species of squid and refusing everything else offered to it.**

An "opportunistic" feeder eats whatever is available at the time, switching prey as circumstances change rather than holding to a fixed diet. Taking one species of squid and refusing all alternatives is the definition of the opposite strategy, and the refusals make the narrowness deliberate rather than accidental. Specialist is the standard term for an animal restricted to a single prey.

A diet of one prey species with everything else declined is specialisation, so the description contradicts the label attached to it.

**C) The flatfish's colouring is "cryptic", breaking up its outline against the gravel so effectively that divers pass within a metre of it.**

In biology, "cryptic" colouring conceals an animal in plain view by matching or disrupting its appearance against the background. The sentence names the mechanism, breaking up the outline against gravel, and gives the evidence that it works in the divers who fail to see it. Note the difference from the everyday sense of cryptic, which means obscure or puzzling rather than camouflaged.

Concealment achieved by pattern rather than by hiding is exactly the biological sense, so the usage fits.

**D) The clownfish is an "obligate" associate of the anemone: away from a host it does not survive long in the wild.**

"Obligate" marks a relationship the organism cannot do without, and it stands in direct contrast to facultative, where the association is possible but optional. The clause after the colon supplies the decisive test: survival fails once the host is removed. The word makes a claim about necessity, not about how often the two are found together.

Dependence strict enough that the animal cannot live without its host is the meaning of the term, so it is applied correctly here.

**E) Tagged individuals show little "senescence", with birds of forty breeding as successfully as birds of twelve.**

"Senescence" is the decline in survival and reproductive performance that comes with age, and it is measured by comparing older animals with younger ones. That comparison is exactly what the sentence provides, and the absence of any gap between forty-year-olds and twelve-year-olds is what justifies "little". Ageing in the loose sense of simply growing older would not do, since the term names the deterioration rather than the passage of time.

Old birds matching young ones on breeding success is what a low rate of senescence looks like, so the term is well used.

tasks.solution_overview: Historical writing grades influence, reliability and novelty, and the vocabulary for each is easy to inflate: a work that shaped everything after it, a story too good to be true, a method built on trial rather than theory, an event with nothing before it. Check the word against the documentary detail the sentence supplies about circulation, corroboration, method or precedent. When the record described is thinner or richer than the word allows, that gap is the point of the item.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Historians call the 1903 pamphlet "seminal", noting that it was never circulated and left no trace in any later design.**

A "seminal" work is one that seeds later work, and the claim is about influence rather than quality or priority. The sentence reports the two facts that make such influence impossible: no circulation at the time and no visible trace in anything designed afterwards. Being first is not enough, since a pamphlet nobody read can be entirely original and still shape nothing that follows.

A text that reached nobody cannot have seeded the field, so the description overreaches — obscure would be the honest word.

**B) The account of the first crossing is "apocryphal", confirmed by three photographs, a dated telegram and four eyewitness statements.**

An "apocryphal" story is widely repeated but of doubtful authenticity, the kind of anecdote that survives because it is satisfying rather than because it is documented. Photographs, a dated telegram and four witness statements are documentation of exactly the sort that removes the doubt. The word passes judgement on the evidence behind a story, not on how often the story is told.

Convergent contemporary documentation is what turns a good story into an established one, so calling this account apocryphal contradicts the evidence beside it.

**C) The designer's approach was "empirical", derived entirely from equations, with no wind-tunnel test or trial flight at any stage.**

An "empirical" method proceeds from observation and experiment, adjusting the design in response to what measurement reveals. Working entirely from equations with no test of any kind is the theoretical route, and the sentence rules out both forms of trial that would have made the work empirical. The two approaches are complementary in aviation history, which is why the distinction is worth keeping sharp.

A design that never met a measurement is theoretical by construction, so the word misdescribes the method it is attached to.

**D) The 1919 flight was reported as "unprecedented", although two other crews had completed the same route in the preceding month.**

"Unprecedented" means that nothing of the kind has happened before, so a single earlier instance is enough to defeat the claim. The concessive clause supplies two, and both are recent and on the same route, which leaves no room for a narrower reading. Remarkable or celebrated would still be available to a writer wanting to convey the achievement.

Two completions of the same route weeks earlier are precedents in the plain sense, so the description cannot stand as written.

**E) Early instrument panels were "rudimentary": an altimeter, a compass, and little else to fly by once cloud closed in.**

"Rudimentary" describes something present only in its most basic form, developed just far enough to be usable. The list after the colon reports exactly that state: two instruments and an acknowledged absence of anything further for flight in cloud. The word concedes that the equipment existed, which is what separates it from saying there was none.

A panel with the barest minimum and nothing beyond it is what the adjective names, so the line holds.

tasks.solution_overview: Agricultural vocabulary carries technical commitments that survive into general prose: what accompanies a change, how genetically uniform a planting is, how many seasons a plant lives, what land can be ploughed, and how much of a harvest leaves the household. Read the descriptive clause and ask which of those commitments it satisfies. Each item here rewards knowing the narrow sense rather than the loose one.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The spread of the potato brought "attendant" risks, dependence on a single crop chief among them, that few observers weighed at the time.**

"Attendant" means accompanying something else as a natural consequence of it, and it nearly always modifies the difficulties or costs that come with a development. The sentence pairs the adoption of the crop with the vulnerability that came alongside it, which is the relationship the adjective asserts. The formal register also suits historical writing of this kind.

Consequences arriving as part of the change itself are what the word describes, so it sits correctly in this sentence.

**B) Planting one clone across whole districts created a "monoculture", uniform enough for a single pathogen to move through it unopposed.**

A "monoculture" is the cultivation of a single crop, and in its strict sense a genetically uniform one, over a large area. Planting one clone district-wide satisfies both readings, and the consequence named — a pathogen meeting no resistant plants — is the classic reason the term matters. Uniformity, not merely scale, is what the word is pointing at.

One clone across whole districts is a monoculture in the most exact sense, so the term is well chosen here.

**C) Unlike wheat, the grass is "perennial", regrowing from the same root system for several seasons without being sown again.**

In botany, "perennial" means living for more than two years, regrowing each season from persistent roots rather than starting again from seed. The sentence gives the definition in working form and sharpens it with the contrast against wheat, which completes its life in a single year. The looser everyday sense, meaning recurrent or perpetual, sits on top of this technical one.

Regrowth from surviving roots over several seasons is precisely what the botanical term specifies, so the usage is right.

**D) Only a narrow strip of the valley floor is "arable"; the slopes above are too thin and stony to take a plough.**

Land is "arable" when it is suitable for growing crops under cultivation, which in practice means it can be ploughed and worked. The semicolon sets up the contrast the term needs, with soil too thin and stony for the plough marking where arable land ends and rough grazing begins. The word describes capability, not what happens to be sown this year.

Ploughable ground set against slopes that cannot be worked is exactly the distinction the term draws, so it fits this sentence.

**E) The household farmed at "subsistence" level, growing enough to feed itself and hardly anything beyond that.**

"Subsistence" farming produces what the household consumes, with little or no surplus, so it names a scale of production rather than a level of skill. The clause after the comma gives that balance exactly: enough to eat, and almost nothing above it. A bad year at this level means hunger rather than a smaller surplus, which is why the term carries such weight in agricultural history.

Production matched to the household's own needs with no margin is the meaning the word carries, so the description holds.

tasks.solution_overview: Manufacturing prose uses words that classify how a process is built and how far along it is: tolerant or unforgiving, separable into parts or welded into one line, made to order or made to a single standard, refined by stages or replaced outright. Read the descriptive clause for the concrete detail — one continuous line, one identical specification, thirty years of production — and hold the word to it. A term about a technology's age is answerable to the record of its use, not to how sophisticated it sounds.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Photolithography is "exacting" work: a particle a fraction of the width of a hair ruins every device on the wafer beneath it.**

"Exacting" describes work that demands great care and accuracy and punishes any lapse in either. The colon supplies the punishment in concrete form, since a speck far smaller than a hair destroys everything on the wafer. The word is about the tolerance the process allows, which is why difficult would be weaker and impossible plainly wrong.

A process that fails at contamination this small is exacting in the fullest sense, so the description is accurate.

**B) The plant's process is "modular", a single continuous line in which no stage can be altered without rebuilding everything downstream of it.**

Something "modular" is built from parts that can be swapped, upgraded or reordered independently, which is the whole practical benefit of the design. The description that follows reports the opposite architecture: one continuous line whose stages are so tightly coupled that changing one forces a rebuild of the rest. Integrated or monolithic is the term for a process with that dependency structure.

Stages that cannot be changed separately are by definition not modules, so the label misdescribes this line — the process is monolithic.

**C) Each mask set is "bespoke", produced to one identical specification and used unchanged in every factory that makes the chip.**

"Bespoke" means made to the particular requirements of a single customer or application, and the register comes from tailoring, where each garment is cut for one person. A single specification reproduced unchanged everywhere is standardisation, which is the opposite production model. The clue is the word "identical", since bespoke items differ from one another by design.

One specification serving every factory alike is standardised rather than made to order, so the word is the wrong one for these mask sets.

**D) Progress in lithography has been "iterative", each generation refining the last rather than replacing it with a different principle.**

An "iterative" development advances by repeated cycles of refinement, with each round starting from the result of the one before. The sentence draws exactly that line, distinguishing successive improvement from the arrival of a new principle. Incremental describes the size of the steps, whereas iterative describes their relationship to one another.

Generation-on-generation refinement of the same approach is what the adjective names, so it characterises this history correctly.

**E) The technique is "nascent", in continuous high-volume production for more than thirty years and present in nearly every household device.**

"Nascent" describes something just coming into existence, still forming, with its eventual shape unsettled. Thirty years of continuous high-volume production and near-universal presence in domestic devices is the profile of a mature technology instead. The word measures how early in its life a technology is, not how advanced it is.

A technique in mass production for three decades is long past its beginnings, so the adjective misplaces it in time — mature is the accurate description.

tasks.solution_overview: Fieldwork writing mixes practical vocabulary with technical terms, and both reward precision: what kind of problem is being solved, what physical process is being named, whether sampling followed a plan or a hunch, and whether a value was read between measurements or beyond them. Take each word to the method or the process it names and check the description against it. Two neighbouring terms that differ only in direction are the hardest to keep apart and the most worth learning.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The expedition's hardest problems were "logistical": fuel, flights and food for eight people camped a hundred kilometres from the nearest road.**

"Logistical" problems concern the organisation and movement of people and supplies rather than the intellectual content of the work. Fuel, flights and food for a party far from any road are that category in its purest form, and the colon presents them as the definition of the difficulty. Scientific problems would be a separate list, which is the contrast the sentence quietly relies on.

Supply and movement for a remote camp is exactly what the adjective covers, so the sentence uses it correctly.

**B) Summer loss from the glacier surface is called "ablation", the melting, evaporation and wind scour that strip metres of ice from the tongue each year.**

In glaciology, "ablation" is the collective term for every process that removes mass from a glacier's surface, which is why the definition lists several mechanisms rather than one. The sentence names melting, evaporation and wind scour, and pairs them with the loss they produce on the tongue. Accumulation is the opposite half of the mass balance, covering snowfall and everything else that adds ice.

Surface loss by all its routes is precisely what the term collects, so the gloss and the word agree.

**C) The team's sampling was "systematic", stopping wherever the ice looked interesting and skipping the stretches that seemed dull.**

"Systematic" sampling follows a rule fixed in advance — every hundred metres, every fifth crevasse — so that the sampler's judgement cannot bias which points enter the record. Stopping where the ice looks interesting is judgement doing exactly that work, and skipping dull stretches removes the very material that would test the pattern. Opportunistic or haphazard is the accurate description of this approach.

Sampling steered by what caught the eye is unsystematic by construction, so the claim does not survive the description that follows it.

**D) Conditions on the plateau are "inhospitable": wind above forty knots for weeks together and temperatures that never climb to freezing.**

"Inhospitable" describes an environment that is hard to live in and offers nothing to sustain those who try. Sustained gale-force wind and temperatures permanently below freezing are the standard evidence for such a judgement, and both are quantified rather than merely asserted. The word applies to places, whereas the related unwelcoming would carry a social sense the sentence does not need.

An environment that provides nothing and punishes a long stay is what the adjective names, so it fits these conditions.

**E) The 1960 value was "extrapolated", read off between two directly measured points that sit on either side of it in the record.**

To "extrapolate" is to project a value beyond the range of the data, which is why extrapolated figures carry the greater risk of the two operations. The description here places the estimate between two measured points, with data on both sides, and that is interpolation.

**Tip:** Direction settles the pair every time: inside the measured range is interpolation, beyond its edges is extrapolation.

A value estimated between two real measurements is interpolated rather than extrapolated, so the term reverses what the record actually supports.

tasks.solution_overview: Deep-sea biology depends on terms that specify an energy source, a spatial pattern, an evolutionary history or a lifespan, and each refuses the neighbouring possibility. Ask what the word commits the organism to — drawing energy from chemistry rather than light, spreading rather than concentrating, shrinking rather than enlarging, arising separately rather than by inheritance — and read the clause that reports the anatomy or behaviour. Several of these words fix a direction of change, so the anatomy described in the sentence is what settles them.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The vent community is "chemosynthetic", built on bacteria that draw their energy from sulphide rather than from sunlight.**

"Chemosynthetic" organisms derive energy from chemical reactions rather than from light, which is what allows entire communities to exist beyond the reach of the sun. The sentence names the compound and states the contrast plainly, so the defining condition is on the page rather than assumed. Photosynthetic communities occupy the other branch of the same distinction.

Energy taken from sulphide instead of sunlight is exactly what the term specifies, so the description is right.

**B) The glow is "diffuse", spread evenly across the animal's underside rather than concentrated in a single organ.**

"Diffuse" describes something spread out over an area rather than gathered at one point, and in descriptions of light it contrasts with a focused or point source. The sentence supplies that contrast in the same breath, setting even distribution across the underside against concentration in one organ. The word says nothing about brightness, only about how the light is distributed.

Even spread rather than a single source is the sense the adjective carries, so it describes this glow accurately.

**C) The fish's eyes are "vestigial", enlarged far beyond the usual proportions to gather the faintest light at depth.**

A "vestigial" structure is a reduced remnant of one that was functional in ancestors, retained in diminished form and usually without its original use. Eyes enlarged beyond the usual proportions and working hard at their job are the opposite case on both counts: bigger, not smaller, and functional rather than residual.

**Trap:** Vestigial reports reduction from an ancestral form, so no structure that has grown larger can qualify, however unusual it looks.

Enlargement in the service of a working function is the negation of vestigial reduction, so the term contradicts the anatomy described.

**D) Light production has evolved along "convergent" paths, appearing independently in squid, fish and jellyfish that share no recent ancestor.**

"Convergent" evolution produces similar traits in lineages that did not inherit them from a common ancestor, usually because similar conditions favour similar solutions. The sentence supplies the two conditions the term requires: independent appearance, and the absence of recent shared ancestry. Traits inherited from a common ancestor would be homologous instead.

Independent arrival at the same solution in unrelated lineages is precisely what the term names, so the wording stands.

**E) A whale-fall community is "ephemeral" on geological timescales, flourishing for a few decades and then disappearing with the last of the bone.**

"Ephemeral" means short-lived, and because duration is always relative the sentence anchors the judgement with an explicit timescale. Decades measured against geological time is brief by any reading, and the community's disappearance with its substrate completes the picture. Without that qualifier the word would be arguable; with it the claim is precise.

A community that lasts decades where the comparison is measured in millions of years is short-lived in the required sense, so the term fits.

tasks.solution_overview: Behavioural research polices its own vocabulary carefully, because each of these terms constrains what may be concluded from a recording: whether a description imports human motives, whether an explanation assumes more than it needs, whether a result has survived independent repetition, whether a behaviour was learned, and which feature the animal actually attended to. Read the methodological detail beside each word and ask what it licenses. Here the terms are used as researchers use them.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The reviewer warned against an "anthropomorphic" reading of the footage, in which the octopus was said to be sulking rather than simply withdrawing.**

An "anthropomorphic" description attributes human feelings or motives to an animal, going beyond the behaviour actually observed. Sulking is a human emotional state, whereas withdrawing is the movement the camera recorded, and the sentence sets one against the other. The warning is a standard one in this literature because such readings quietly smuggle in a conclusion.

Reading a human mood into an animal's movement is exactly the error the term names, so the reviewer's word is well chosen.

**B) The "parsimonious" explanation is learning by association; nothing in the recordings requires the animal to be planning several moves ahead.**

A "parsimonious" explanation is the one that accounts for the observations while assuming the least, a principle with particular force in comparative psychology. The semicolon supplies the reasoning: association covers what the recordings show, and the richer account of forward planning is not required by any of it. Parsimony is a standard for choosing between explanations, not a claim that the simpler one is certainly true.

Choosing the account that explains the data with the fewest added assumptions is precisely what the word describes, so it is used correctly here.

**C) The result counts as "replicable": two other laboratories ran the same protocol on new animals and reported the same outcome.**

A finding is "replicable" when the same procedure, carried out afresh, produces the same result. The colon supplies both requirements: independent laboratories rather than the original team, and new animals rather than the original sample. Reanalysing the same dataset would be reproducibility, a weaker and quite different check.

Independent repetition yielding the same outcome is what the term certifies, so the sentence applies it properly.

**D) The escape response appears "innate", performed correctly by animals raised in isolation that had never seen it done.**

A behaviour is "innate" when it develops without the relevant experience, which is why isolation rearing is the standard test. The sentence describes that design and reports its result: correct performance by animals with no opportunity to learn the behaviour from others. The hedge "appears" is appropriate, since such conclusions rest on the adequacy of the deprivation.

Correct performance without any chance to learn it is the evidence the term demands, so the word is used as researchers use it.

**E) In these trials the lid's handle was the "salient" feature, the one detail the animal returned to on every attempt.**

"Salient" marks the feature that stands out and captures attention, which in behavioural work is measured by what the animal actually attends to. The appositive gives that measurement: the handle is the detail returned to on every attempt, not merely the one an observer finds obvious. Salience is a property of the animal's engagement with the display rather than of the display alone.

The feature the animal went back to each time is the salient one by any working definition, so the term fits these trials.

tasks.solution_overview: Economic terms sound familiar and mean something narrower: how quickly an asset converts to cash, how far quantity responds to price, whether assets cover obligations, whether spending can be postponed, and how a policy behaves over the cycle. Each item supplies the number or the fact that the definition demands, so read that detail before accepting the label. Two of these words are routinely swapped in ordinary speech, and the sentences here are built to separate them.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The bank described the holding as "liquid", a stake in an unlisted company that took eleven months to sell.**

An asset is "liquid" when it can be converted into cash quickly and at a predictable price, which is why deposits and government bills are the standard examples. A stake in an unlisted company that took eleven months to find a buyer fails on both counts, since neither the timing nor the price was dependable. Illiquid is the term for a holding of exactly this kind.

Eleven months to reach a sale is the opposite of ready convertibility, so the description does not hold — the stake was illiquid.

**B) Demand for the drug is "elastic", with the quantity bought unchanged after the price tripled.**

Demand is "elastic" when quantity responds sharply to price, so a large price movement should produce a proportionally larger fall in the amount bought. Here the price tripled and the quantity did not move at all, which is the textbook picture of the opposite case. Inelastic demand is characteristic of goods with no substitute, which is why essential medicines are the standard illustration.

Quantity that ignores a tripling in price is inelastic by definition, so the label reverses what the figures show.

**C) The auditors pronounced the company "solvent" while recording liabilities that exceeded the value of everything it owned.**

Solvency is a comparison of stocks: a firm is "solvent" when its assets are worth at least as much as its obligations. Liabilities exceeding the value of all assets is the accounting definition of insolvency, whatever cash may happen to be in the account this week.

**Trap:** Solvency compares what is owned with what is owed; liquidity asks only whether today's bills can be met, and a firm can pass one test while failing the other.

Obligations larger than total assets is insolvency on the face of the accounts, so the judgement recorded here cannot stand.

**D) Spending on rent and heating was classified as "discretionary", the part of a household budget that cannot be deferred.**

"Discretionary" spending is what a household chooses to do and can drop when money is short, which is precisely why it falls first in a downturn. The gloss offered in apposition describes the other category altogether: commitments that cannot be postponed, of which rent and heating are the usual examples. Non-discretionary or committed expenditure is the term the definition is reaching for.

Spending that cannot be deferred is committed rather than discretionary, so the classification and its own gloss contradict each other.

**E) Unemployment insurance is "countercyclical" by construction, paying out most at exactly the point when output is contracting.**

A "countercyclical" measure moves against the economic cycle, expanding when activity falls and shrinking when it recovers. Unemployment insurance does this automatically, since claims rise as output contracts, which is why it is the standard example of an automatic stabiliser. A procyclical policy would do the reverse and deepen the downturn.

Payments that swell precisely as output falls run counter to the cycle in the technical sense, so the term is used correctly.

tasks.solution_overview: Spacecraft reporting turns on where a decision is taken, how a resource behaves over time, how faint a signal is, how value accrues and how a discovery came about. Each word asserts one of those things and can be checked against the operational detail attached to it. Watch in particular for absolute claims, which a single measured detail in the same sentence is often enough to overturn.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The craft's course corrections are "autonomous", each one computed on Earth and uploaded days before the engine may fire.**

An "autonomous" system decides for itself, without waiting for instructions from outside, which is why autonomy matters most where the signal delay is long. The description here places every decision on the ground and reduces the spacecraft to executing an instruction it was sent. Automated is the accurate word for a sequence carried out without human intervention but not chosen by the machine.

Manoeuvres computed on Earth and uploaded in advance are commanded rather than self-directed, so the description overstates what the craft decides.

**B) The probe's plutonium source is "inexhaustible", losing a measurable fraction of its output every year since launch.**

"Inexhaustible" is an absolute claim: the supply never runs down, however long it is drawn on. A source whose output falls by a measurable fraction annually is doing exactly what exhaustion looks like, slowly and predictably, and mission planners schedule instrument shutdowns around it. Long-lived would carry the intended admiration without the false absolute.

Steady annual decline is depletion in progress, so the adjective claims more than the record allows — long-lived is the defensible word.

**C) The radio link is "tenuous": a fraction of a watt, gathered after twenty hours of travel by antennas seventy metres across.**

"Tenuous" describes something thin, slight and easily lost, and applied to a connection it suggests one maintained only by extraordinary effort. The figures after the colon supply exactly that impression: a signal of a fraction of a watt, and dishes of seventy metres needed to hear it at all. The word carries no suggestion that the link is unreliable, only that it is faint.

A connection this slight, held open only by enormous receiving power, is tenuous in the exact sense, so the wording fits.

**D) The mission's value is "cumulative", each further decade of measurement gaining meaning from the decades already recorded.**

Something is "cumulative" when its total grows by successive additions and each addition builds on what came before. The sentence states that relationship rather than merely asserting growth, since new measurements draw their meaning from the existing record. Long baselines in space physics behave in precisely this way, which is why old data keep gaining value.

Value that accrues by addition and depends on the record already held is what the adjective describes, so it is used correctly.

**E) The detection of the boundary was partly "serendipitous", made by an instrument built to answer an entirely different question.**

A "serendipitous" discovery is a valuable one arrived at while looking for something else, which is why the word implies luck and alertness together. The sentence supplies the mismatch the term depends on, between the instrument's intended question and the result it delivered. Accidental would cover the luck but lose the sense of a fortunate outcome.

A useful finding produced by an instrument aimed elsewhere is serendipity in its proper sense, so the description holds.

tasks.solution_overview: Publishing vocabulary describes procedures, and each term names a condition that a described process either satisfies or fails: identities concealed from both sides, assessment before posting, absence of a stake in the outcome, a claim held open, a search that missed nothing. Read the procedural detail and ask whether the condition survives it. One of these words is regularly confused with a near neighbour that differs by a single prefix and means something else entirely.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The journal calls its assessment "double-blind", while printing each author's name and institution at the head of every manuscript sent out for review.**

A "double-blind" review conceals the authors from the reviewers and the reviewers from the authors, so neither side knows who the other is. Printing names and institutions at the head of the manuscript removes half of that concealment before the reviewer has read a line. Single-blind is the term for the arrangement the sentence actually describes.

Author identities visible on the first page defeat one of the two blinds, so the journal's description of its own process is inaccurate.

**B) The preprint was cited as "peer-reviewed", although it had simply been posted to a public server that accepts uploads without assessment.**

"Peer-reviewed" means specialists in the field have evaluated the work and a journal has acted on their reports before publication. A server that accepts uploads without assessment applies no such filter, which is the whole point of preprints and the reason they are labelled as such. The status is about the process a paper has passed through, not about where readers can find it.

Posting without any expert evaluation leaves the paper unreviewed, so the citation claims a status the work has not yet acquired.

**C) The assessor was described as "disinterested", having co-authored four papers with the applicant in the previous two years.**

"Disinterested" means having no stake in the outcome, which is the quality that makes a judgement trustworthy. Four recent co-authored papers create precisely the stake the word denies, since the assessor's own record is bound up with the applicant's standing. Conflicted is the term panels use for exactly this situation.

**Trap:** Disinterested is not uninterested: the first describes the absence of a stake, the second the absence of curiosity.

A recent collaborator has an interest in the result, so the description cannot stand — the assessor was conflicted rather than disinterested.

**D) The finding was published as "provisional", with the authors flagging a sample too small to settle the question either way.**

A result offered as "provisional" is put forward for the time being, on the understanding that further evidence may change it. The sentence supplies both the hedge and its stated ground, since the authors themselves name the sample size as the limitation. The word describes the standing of the claim rather than any doubt about the honesty of the work.

A claim published subject to revision, with the reason stated, is provisional in the exact sense, so the wording holds.

**E) The literature search was "exhaustive", covering every relevant database, publications in four languages, and unpublished theses as well.**

An "exhaustive" search leaves nothing out within its stated scope, which is a stronger claim than thorough and one that reviewers test. The list supplies the three coverage gaps that usually defeat such claims — databases, languages and unpublished work — and closes all of them. The word describes completeness of coverage, not the length of the resulting reference list.

Coverage that closes the usual escape routes is what the adjective asserts, so it is justified by the description given.

tasks.solution_overview: Data governance runs on words that must survive being tested: whether individuals can still be picked out, whether a system can explain itself, whether a third factor drives both sides of a correlation, whether an intrusion is balanced against its purpose, and how finely a dataset resolves. Read what the record or the system actually contains and compare it with the claim the term makes. A dataset is answerable to the fields it actually holds, whatever label has been placed on the file.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The release was described as "anonymised", with every record still carrying a full postcode, a date of birth and a sex.**

Data are "anonymised" only when individuals can no longer be identified from them, directly or by combination with other available information. Postcode, date of birth and sex is the classic trio shown to single out most people in a population, so the records remain identifiable in practice. Pseudonymised is the accurate term for data with names removed but re-identification still possible.

Fields that between them pick out individuals leave the release identifiable, so the label overstates the protection actually applied.

**B) The model is "opaque" even to the team that trained it: it returns a score with no account of the features that produced it.**

An "opaque" system is one whose internal workings cannot be seen through, so its outputs arrive without an accessible explanation. The colon gives that condition exactly: a score is produced, and the reasoning behind it is unavailable even to the builders. Interpretable systems sit at the other end of the same scale, which is why the pairing is standard in this literature.

An output with no visible route from inputs to score is opaque in the intended sense, so the description is apt.

**C) The correlation is "confounded" by household wealth, which drives both the exposure under study and the outcome being measured.**

A relationship is "confounded" when a third variable influences both of the things being compared, producing an association that is not causal. The relative clause states that structure precisely: wealth acts on the exposure and on the outcome alike. A variable affecting only the outcome would not confound anything, which is why the double link matters.

A common cause standing behind both sides of the correlation is the definition of confounding, so the term is used correctly.

**D) The regulator asked whether the surveillance was "proportionate", weighing the intrusion into private life against the seriousness of the offence being investigated.**

"Proportionate" in regulatory usage means no more intrusive than the objective requires, and the assessment is always a comparison between two named quantities. The sentence supplies both sides of that balance, the intrusion and the gravity of the offence, which is how the test is actually applied. Reasonable would be vaguer and would lose the explicit weighing the word implies.

Measuring the intrusion against the purpose it serves is exactly the exercise the term describes, so it fits this question.

**E) The location data is "granular" enough to distinguish one flat from the next, not merely one district from another.**

"Granular" data is recorded in fine units, so that small distinctions survive rather than being averaged away. The sentence measures that fineness by contrast, setting the flat against the district and letting the reader see the resolution. Detailed would be looser, since granularity is specifically about the size of the unit in which the data is held.

Resolution fine enough to separate neighbouring flats is granularity in the exact sense, so the term is well applied.

tasks.solution_overview: Constitutional vocabulary distinguishes what a court can decide, what a constitution protects from ordinary change, what a power actually authorises, when a ruling takes effect, and how much weight a foreign judgment carries. Each term names a limit, so read the clause that describes the limit and check that the two agree. These items reward knowing the Latin phrases as working tests rather than as decoration.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The court held that the question was not "justiciable", since it turned on political judgement rather than on any legal standard a judge could apply.**

A question is "justiciable" when it can properly be decided by a court, which requires legal standards a judge is equipped to apply. The reason given is the classic ground for holding otherwise: a matter resolvable only by political judgement offers the court nothing to measure the decision against. The holding is about the court's competence, not about the merits of either side.

Absence of any applicable legal standard is precisely what makes a question non-justiciable, so the reasoning and the term match.

**B) The clause is "entrenched": amending it requires a two-thirds majority and a referendum, not the ordinary legislative vote.**

An "entrenched" provision is protected against ordinary amendment by a heavier procedure than normal legislation demands. The colon supplies that procedure and contrasts it with the ordinary vote, which is exactly the comparison the term depends on. Entrenchment concerns the difficulty of change, not whether the provision may be changed at all.

A special majority and a referendum are entrenchment in operation, so the term describes this clause accurately.

**C) The order was quashed as "ultra vires", having been made under a power the statute never conferred on the minister.**

An act is "ultra vires" when it goes beyond the powers actually granted, and in administrative law that grant is traced to the statute. The participial clause identifies the defect precisely: the minister acted under an authority the legislation did not provide. The complaint is about the existence of the power rather than the wisdom of its use.

Acting outside a power the statute never granted is the whole content of the phrase, so it names this defect correctly.

**D) The ruling was given "prospective" effect only, leaving decisions already taken under the old interpretation undisturbed.**

A judgment with "prospective" effect governs conduct from the ruling onwards and does not reopen what was settled before it. The sentence names the consequence that follows from that limitation, since earlier decisions stand. Retrospective effect is the alternative, and courts limit themselves in this way precisely to protect arrangements already made.

Forward-looking operation that leaves past decisions intact is what the term specifies, so the sentence uses it correctly.

**E) Judgments of the foreign court are "persuasive" rather than binding: they may be cited and followed, but nothing obliges a judge to do so.**

"Persuasive" authority may influence a decision by the strength of its reasoning, while binding authority must be followed because of where it sits in the hierarchy. The colon states both halves of that distinction, and the word "obliges" marks the line between them. Foreign judgments are the standard example, since no domestic court is subordinate to them.

Authority that may convince but cannot compel is exactly what the term denotes, so the description is right.

tasks.solution_overview: Trial vocabulary is written to prevent wishful reading: allocation by chance rather than by judgement, a difference that matters to a patient rather than one that merely reaches a threshold, the share of cases owed to an exposure, harm caused by the treatment itself, and disease that resists it. Read the procedural or numerical detail and ask whether the term's condition is met. Where the described facts belong to a neighbouring term, that term is the one the sentence should have used.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The study was called "randomised", although clinicians assigned each patient to an arm themselves after reviewing the scan results.**

A trial is "randomised" when allocation to arms is decided by chance, which is what keeps known and unknown differences between groups from following the clinician's judgement. Assignment made by clinicians who have seen the scans is allocation by judgement, and it reintroduces exactly the bias randomisation exists to remove. Such a design is a controlled comparison, but not a randomised one.

Allocation steered by the clinician's reading of the scans is the antithesis of chance assignment, so the study cannot be described this way.

**B) The two-hour reduction was reported as "clinically significant", a change that patients could not perceive and that altered no treatment decision.**

A result is "clinically significant" when the difference is large enough to matter to patients or to change what clinicians do. The appositive rules out both tests at once: imperceptible to patients, and inert as far as treatment decisions go.

**Tip:** Statistical significance asks whether a difference is real; clinical significance asks whether it is big enough to matter, and a large enough trial can deliver the first without the second.

A change nobody notices and nothing turns on fails the clinical test whatever the p-value, so the description overstates the finding.

**C) A fifth of the cases were "attributable" to the exposure, that being the share which would not have occurred had it been absent.**

In epidemiology the "attributable" fraction is the proportion of cases that would not have arisen without the exposure, which is a causal quantity rather than a simple count. The relative clause states that counterfactual definition directly, which is what distinguishes it from the share of cases in which the exposure is merely present. The distinction matters because many exposed cases would have occurred anyway.

Defining the fraction by what would not have happened otherwise is exactly the technical sense, so the term is used correctly.

**D) The infection was recorded as "iatrogenic", having been traced to contaminated well water at the patient's home.**

An "iatrogenic" condition is caused by medical examination or treatment, which is why the category is used to audit care rather than the environment. Contaminated well water at home locates the source outside the health system entirely, and the tracing makes that origin definite. Community-acquired is the classification such a case receives.

An origin in the patient's own water supply owes nothing to medical treatment, so the record applies the wrong category here.

**E) The tumour was described as "refractory", having disappeared entirely after the first course of treatment.**

In oncology, "refractory" disease resists treatment, either failing to respond at all or progressing while therapy continues. Complete disappearance after a first course is the strongest possible response, and the word for it is responsive, with a complete response the recorded outcome. The everyday sense of refractory, meaning stubborn or unmanageable, points the same way and should have warned the writer off.

A tumour that vanished at the first attempt resisted nothing, so the description is the reverse of what the case shows.

tasks.solution_overview: Diplomatic vocabulary records who acted, on what terms, and with what standing in law: a step taken alone or by agreement, a line existing in practice or established in law, a process that dragged, a gesture that softened. Read the clause that reports how many parties were involved and what instrument, if any, stands behind the arrangement. Two Latin tags in this area differ only in whether formal recognition exists, and one of them is tested here.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Recognition of the new government was "conditional", withheld until the promised elections had actually taken place.**

Something "conditional" takes effect only if a stated requirement is met, so the condition governs whether the act happens at all. The sentence names the requirement and the consequence of not meeting it, since recognition was held back pending the elections. Unconditional recognition would have followed regardless of what the new authorities did next.

Recognition suspended until a stated event occurs is conditional in the exact sense, so the wording stands.

**B) The withdrawal was presented as "unilateral", although it had been settled in advance with both neighbouring states and written into a joint declaration.**

A "unilateral" act is taken by one party alone, without the agreement of the others affected, which is what gives such acts their political force and their risk. Prior settlement with two neighbouring states, recorded in a joint declaration, is agreement in the fullest documentary sense. Multilateral or negotiated is the accurate description of a step arranged this way.

A move agreed in advance and set down jointly cannot be one party acting alone, so the presentation misdescribes what happened.

**C) The dividing line was described as "de facto", though it had been fixed by a ratified treaty and is recognised by every state in the region.**

A "de facto" arrangement exists in practice without formal legal recognition, which is why ceasefire lines and armistice boundaries attract the phrase. A ratified treaty accepted by every state in the region supplies precisely the legal recognition the term denies.

**Tip:** Keep the pair by their test: de facto asks what is happening on the ground, de jure asks what an instrument says.

A boundary founded on a ratified treaty holds in law and not merely in fact, so the tag chosen here is the wrong one of the pair.

**D) The negotiations were "protracted", running through nine rounds across four years before any text was initialled.**

"Protracted" describes something drawn out over far more time than expected or than seems necessary, and it carries a hint of weariness. Nine rounds across four years before even an initialled text is that experience quantified, with the delay measured against the modest result achieved. Lengthy would be neutral, whereas protracted registers the strain.

Four years of rounds before a first initialled text is a negotiation drawn out in exactly the way the word implies, so the description fits.

**E) The closing speech was "conciliatory", conceding a point the delegation had defended for a decade and inviting the other side to answer in kind.**

A "conciliatory" gesture is intended to end hostility and win the other side over, usually by giving ground rather than by demanding it. Both halves of the sentence supply that content: a long-defended position surrendered, and an invitation to reciprocate. Emollient language alone would not be enough, since the word implies a real move towards the opponent.

A genuine concession paired with an invitation to reply in kind is conciliation in practice, so the adjective is well chosen.

tasks.solution_overview: Evaluation vocabulary is built to keep claims honest: what happens when nobody chooses, what the comparison group stands for, whether pressure was really applied, how far a result may travel, and when the analysis plan was fixed. Each term names a condition, and each sentence reports enough of the design to test it. Where the reported design fails the condition, the write-up has claimed a standard the study did not meet.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Enrolment operates by "default": eligible residents are placed in the scheme automatically and stay in it unless they ask to leave.**

A "default" is the outcome that takes effect when a person makes no active choice, which is why defaults exert such influence on participation rates. The colon describes that arrangement precisely: automatic placement, with continued membership for anyone who does nothing. An opt-in scheme would reverse the default and leave inaction meaning non-participation.

Automatic inclusion unless the person acts is the definition of an opt-out default, so the term is used correctly here.
