**B) The evaluation rests on a "counterfactual", an estimate of what the same households would have done had no appointment reminder arrived.**

A "counterfactual" is a statement of what would have happened under conditions that did not in fact obtain, and every claim about an effect depends on one. The appositive states that structure exactly, since the comparison is with the same households in a world without the reminder. The counterfactual is estimated rather than observed, which is why control groups exist.

An estimate of the unobserved alternative course of events is what the term names, so the sentence uses it properly.

**C) The reminder letter was criticised as "coercive", although recipients faced no penalty of any kind and could ignore it without consequence.**

Coercion works by removing acceptable alternatives, typically through force, threat or penalty, so the person is left with no real option but to comply. The concessive clause withdraws exactly that element: no penalty, and no consequence for ignoring the letter. Nudges may still be criticised as manipulative, which is a different and more interesting objection.

A letter that can be binned without cost leaves the choice intact, so the criticism reaches for a word the facts do not support.

**D) The finding was presented as "generalisable", having been obtained on a single street in one town and never tested anywhere else.**

A result is "generalisable" when there is reason to expect it to hold beyond the particular sample and setting that produced it, which usually means variation across sites or populations. One street in one town, never replicated, provides no such variation and no evidence about other contexts. Internally valid is the most such a study can claim: it may describe that street accurately and say nothing about anywhere else.

A single untested site supplies no ground for extending the result, so the presentation claims a reach the design cannot support.

**E) The analysis was described as "pre-registered", with the primary outcome chosen after the team had examined the collected data.**

"Pre-registration" means the hypotheses and analysis plan are lodged publicly before the data are seen, which is what stops the outcome measure from being selected to fit the result. Choosing the primary outcome after looking at the data is the practice pre-registration exists to prevent. An exploratory analysis is a legitimate thing to report, provided it is labelled as one.

An outcome selected once the data were in hand cannot have been registered in advance, so the description claims a safeguard the study did not apply.

tasks.solution_overview: Resistance policy has its own precise vocabulary: governing how drugs are used, the pressure that favours resistant strains, the reserve agent held back, the breadth of an agent's coverage, and the route by which resistance genes travel. Read the clinical or biological detail beside each term and ask whether it satisfies the condition the word sets. Timing matters as much as meaning here: what was already known when the choice was made, and what had already been tried.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The hospital calls the programme "stewardship", governing which agents may be used, at what dose, for how long and on whose authority.**

"Stewardship" describes the careful management of a shared resource on behalf of others, and antimicrobial stewardship applies that idea to drugs whose effectiveness is depleted by use. The list of controls gives the programme its substance: agent, dose, duration and authorisation, the four levers such schemes actually pull. The word carries the sense of holding something in trust rather than merely restricting it.

Managing a shared and exhaustible resource through explicit controls is exactly what the term denotes, so it fits this programme.

**B) Routine dosing across a herd applies "selective pressure", handing an advantage to any resistant strain in every generation that follows.**

"Selective pressure" is any factor that makes some variants reproduce more successfully than others, so that their frequency rises over generations. Continuous antibiotic exposure is the textbook case, since susceptible bacteria are removed and resistant ones inherit the space. The phrase describes a differential advantage rather than the creation of a mutation.

Continuous exposure that favours resistant variants generation after generation is selection in the strict sense, so the phrase is correctly used.

**C) Colistin is treated as a "last-resort" agent, held back for infections that every other available antibiotic has failed to clear.**

A "last-resort" drug is kept in reserve for cases where the alternatives have already been tried and have failed, which is why access to it is restricted rather than encouraged. The sentence states both parts of that policy: deliberate withholding, and the clinical situation that releases it. Reserving such agents preserves their usefulness by limiting the exposure that breeds resistance.

An agent held back until everything else has failed is a last resort in the literal sense, so the description holds.

**D) The prescription was defended as "broad-spectrum", chosen because the laboratory had already identified the single organism responsible.**

A "broad-spectrum" antibiotic acts against a wide range of bacteria, which is why it is the right choice while the organism is still unknown. Once the laboratory has named the organism, prescribing practice moves the other way, to the narrowest agent that covers it, precisely to spare everything else. The reason offered here therefore argues against the choice it is meant to justify.

A known organism calls for narrow targeted therapy rather than wide coverage, so the defence undercuts itself.

**E) Resistance also spreads by "horizontal" transfer, passing between unrelated bacteria rather than only from a cell to its descendants.**

"Horizontal" gene transfer moves genetic material sideways between organisms that are not parent and offspring, often across species boundaries. The sentence supplies the contrast that defines the term, setting transfer between unrelated bacteria against inheritance down a line of descent. Vertical transmission is the name for that second route.

Movement between unrelated cells rather than along a line of descent is exactly what the term specifies, so it is used correctly.

tasks.solution_overview: Migration research needs words for faithfulness to a place, steady loss from a sample, the geometry of a route, irregular mass movements and sheer scale. Each is answerable to a number or a pattern in the record, so read the figures attached to it. Where the tagging data show the exact behaviour the term specifies, the technical word is doing work that a general one could not.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The birds show strong site "fidelity", returning to the same ledge within a metre or so year after year.**

Site "fidelity" is the tendency of an animal to return to the same location across seasons or years, and its strength is measured by how precisely the return is made. The sentence supplies that measurement, since a metre on the same ledge is about as exact as such returns get. The word describes attachment to a place rather than to a mate, which is a separate use of the same term.

Precise annual return to one spot is the behaviour the term names, so it is applied correctly here.

**B) The tag record shows steady "attrition", with fewer transmitters reporting in each successive month of the crossing.**

"Attrition" is gradual loss from a group by a continuing process rather than a single event, whether through failure, detachment or death. Month-by-month decline in the number of reporting tags fits that pattern exactly, and the word is standard in describing sample loss over a study. A sudden collapse in reports would need a different account, since attrition implies erosion.

Steady month-on-month loss from the reporting sample is attrition in the ordinary technical sense, so the description holds.

**C) The route is "circumpolar", carrying the birds right around the southern ocean rather than back and forth along one meridian.**

"Circumpolar" describes a distribution or a track that encircles one of the poles, and the sentence makes the geometry explicit by contrast. Travelling around the southern ocean is circular movement about the pole, whereas a there-and-back journey along a single meridian would be latitudinal. The word describes the shape of the route, not its length.

A track that goes right around the pole is circumpolar in the plain geographical sense, so the term fits.

**D) Movements of the species are "irruptive": in most winters the birds stay north, and in a few they appear far south in enormous numbers.**

An "irruptive" species moves in occasional mass irruptions rather than on a regular annual schedule, usually when food supplies fail. The colon reports that irregularity in the form ornithologists use: most years nothing, occasional years an enormous influx. Regular migration would show the same journey each season, which is the pattern the sentence rules out.

Occasional mass movements against a background of staying put is precisely what the term describes, so the wording stands.

**E) The distances are "prodigious", with one tagged bird logging ninety thousand kilometres in a single year.**

"Prodigious" means impressively great in extent, and the word carries a note of astonishment that ordinary large does not. Ninety thousand kilometres in a year is more than twice around the planet, which is the kind of figure the adjective exists for. The sentence earns the word by supplying the number rather than leaving the reader to take the claim on trust.

A single year's travel of that magnitude is remarkable by any measure, so the adjective is justified here.

tasks.solution_overview: Conservation vocabulary carries strict commitments: whether a treatment can be undone, what has built up on a surface, how complete an object's documented history is, what kind of imitation a forgery attempts, and what is missing from a paint layer. Read the factual clause and ask whether it satisfies the condition or quietly cancels it. Documented history is judged by whether the chain of records is unbroken, not by how confident the report sounds.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The treatment is described as "reversible", using an adhesive that cannot be removed later without lifting the paint layer with it.**

A "reversible" treatment can be undone without damage, leaving the object as it was before, which is why reversibility is a founding principle of modern conservation. An adhesive that takes the paint with it fails that test in the most direct way available, since the removal itself causes the loss. Irreversible interventions are sometimes accepted, but they are never described this way.

A treatment that destroys the paint on removal cannot be undone, so the description claims exactly what the material rules out.

**B) Centuries of "accretion" had darkened the surface: varnish, soot, and successive layers of well-meant retouching.**

"Accretion" is material added gradually in layers over time, and in conservation it names everything that has accumulated on a surface since the artist left it. The list after the colon is exactly that inventory, mixing deliberate additions with accidental deposits. Accretion is distinct from the original paint, which is why removing it is a defensible aim.

Layer upon layer added over centuries is precisely what the noun describes, so it fits this surface.

**C) The panel's "provenance" is secure, with nothing at all known of its whereabouts between 1620 and its reappearance in a private collection in 1932.**

"Provenance" is the documented chain of ownership and location from the object's creation to the present, and its security depends on that chain being unbroken. A gap of three centuries is the largest possible break, and gaps of this kind are exactly where losses and forgeries are hidden. Attribution is a separate question, since a work can be confidently attributed and still have a broken provenance.

Three unrecorded centuries leave the chain of ownership open at its widest point, so the provenance is anything but secure.

**D) The forgery is a "pastiche" in the strict sense, invented wholly from the forger's imagination without reference to any earlier work.**

A "pastiche" is assembled from borrowed elements, imitating the manner of an artist or combining motifs taken from existing works. Invention owing nothing to any earlier work is the opposite procedure, since there is nothing borrowed to assemble. Such a piece might be a forgery in style, but it is an original composition rather than a pastiche.

A work that copies nothing has no borrowed parts to assemble, so the strict sense of the term cannot apply to it.

**E) A "lacuna" runs across the sitter's hand, a loss where the paint layer has gone entirely and only ground remains.**

A "lacuna" is a gap where original material is missing, whether in a manuscript, a mosaic or a paint film. The appositive gives the condition that qualifies it here: the paint layer has gone, leaving bare ground rather than damaged pigment. Abrasion or discoloured retouching would be different conditions, since in both cases some original material survives.

Total loss of the paint layer down to the ground is a lacuna in the conservator's sense, so the term is used properly.

tasks.solution_overview: Conservation genetics uses terms that specify how seed behaves in storage, where a variety came from, how uniformly it breeds, whether it can still germinate and where it is being kept. Each word sets a condition, and each sentence supplies the germination result, the breeding behaviour or the storage arrangement that tests it. A technical sense can run against the everyday one, so let the reported detail decide rather than the word's ordinary flavour.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Cocoa seed is "recalcitrant": it cannot be dried and frozen as wheat can, and dies within weeks of leaving the pod.**

In seed science, "recalcitrant" is a technical classification for seed that does not survive drying and freezing, in contrast to orthodox seed, which does. The colon supplies both halves of that definition: conventional storage is impossible, and viability is lost within weeks. The everyday sense of stubborn resistance survives faintly, since such species resist the standard method.

Seed that cannot be dried or frozen and dies quickly is recalcitrant in the exact technical sense, so the term is right.

**B) The collection preserves a "landrace", a local population shaped over generations by farmers rather than bred at a research station.**

A "landrace" is a traditional variety developed through generations of farmer selection in one locality, and it is typically diverse rather than uniform. The appositive states both defining features, the local origin and the absence of formal breeding, and sets them against the modern cultivar. Landraces matter to seed banks precisely because they carry variation that formal breeding has narrowed.

Farmer selection in a particular place over generations is the whole content of the term, so it is correctly applied.

**C) The hybrid line is "true-breeding", producing a second generation that varies widely from the parent plants in height and yield.**

A "true-breeding" line produces offspring resembling the parents in the traits concerned, generation after generation, because the relevant loci are homozygous. Wide variation appearing in the second generation is the classic signature of a hybrid segregating, which is the opposite behaviour. It is the reason farmers cannot save seed from hybrid varieties and expect the same crop.

Offspring that scatter away from the parental type are not breeding true, so the description defeats the label attached to it.

**D) The accession was logged as "viable" after a germination test in which none of the two hundred seeds sprouted.**

Seed is "viable" when it is alive and capable of germinating, and the germination test is exactly the procedure used to establish that. A test in which no seed out of two hundred sprouted is the strongest available evidence for the opposite conclusion. Viability is a matter of measured germination rather than of how the seed looks or how carefully it has been stored.

A germination rate of zero is the record of a dead accession, so the entry contradicts the test it claims to rest on.

**E) Some varieties are conserved "in situ", left growing in the fields where they developed rather than held as frozen samples.**

"In situ" conservation keeps organisms in the place where they occur, so that they continue to adapt in their original setting. The sentence supplies the contrast on which the term depends, setting living fields against frozen storage, which is the ex situ alternative. The phrase describes location rather than method, and the two strategies are usually pursued together.

Maintaining varieties in their original growing places is exactly what the phrase specifies, so it fits this description.

tasks.solution_overview: Control regimes depend on terms of art: goods with both civilian and military application, rules that reach conduct abroad, single points through which everything must pass, measures answering measures, and prohibitions with or without a legal basis. Read the clause describing where the rule bites, what the item is used for, and whether anything was written into law. Two Latin tags in this field differ only on that last point, and one of them is tested here.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The microscope was listed as "dual-use", though it has no application beyond routine hospital diagnosis.**

A "dual-use" item is one with both civilian and military or weapons-related applications, which is precisely why such items attract export control. An instrument with no application beyond hospital diagnosis has a single civilian use and fails the definition at the first step. The listing decision may still be arguable, but not on this ground.

One civilian application and nothing else leaves no second use to speak of, so the classification does not fit this instrument.

**B) The rule was described as "extraterritorial", applying only to conduct that takes place inside the issuing state's own borders.**

An "extraterritorial" rule reaches conduct beyond the borders of the state that made it, which is what makes such rules diplomatically contentious. A measure confined to conduct at home is ordinary domestic regulation and raises none of those questions. The word describes the geographical reach of a rule, not how strict it is.

A rule that stops at the border reaches nothing extraterritorially, so the description misstates its scope.

**C) One factory has become a "chokepoint": nearly every advanced design in the world must pass through its machines at some stage.**

A "chokepoint" is a narrow passage through which traffic must pass, so that whoever controls it controls the flow; the term moved from geography into supply-chain analysis without changing shape. The colon supplies the two features that define it, a single point and no way around it. That is why chokepoints attract regulatory attention out of all proportion to their size.

A single unavoidable passage that everything must go through is a chokepoint in the exact sense, so the term is well used.

**D) The controls were presented as "reciprocal", imposed on a state that had taken no comparable measure against the country imposing them.**

"Reciprocal" measures answer equivalent measures taken by the other side, and the mutuality is the whole justification for the word. The sentence removes that basis by reporting that the other state had taken no comparable step, which leaves the controls first in the sequence rather than answering anything. Unilateral or pre-emptive would describe what actually happened.

There is nothing to reciprocate when the other side has not acted at all, so the presentation dresses a first move as a reply.

**E) The prohibition is "de jure" only, resting on informal pressure from officials with nothing whatever written into law.**

A "de jure" prohibition exists in law, set down in an instrument that can be pointed to, challenged and enforced through the courts. Informal pressure with nothing written down is the opposite footing: the restriction operates in practice while having no legal existence at all. De facto is the tag for a situation that holds in fact without legal foundation.

A ban that exists only in officials' behaviour has no legal basis to appeal to, so the Latin tag chosen here is the wrong one of the pair.

tasks.solution_overview: Modelling vocabulary states what kind of claim is being made: one outcome or a distribution of them, a response proportional to its cause or not, a path that retraces itself or does not, a process resolved directly or represented by a rule, and a scenario that is possible rather than expected. Read the methodological detail beside each word and hold the term to it. How a model treats uncertainty is declared by the form of its output, so read that form before accepting the label.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The projection is "deterministic", presented as a spread of two thousand runs with a probability attached to each outcome.**

A "deterministic" model returns a single outcome for a given set of inputs, with no randomness in the process and no distribution at the end. Two thousand runs with probabilities attached to the outcomes is the signature of a probabilistic or ensemble approach, built precisely to represent uncertainty. The distinction concerns how the model treats uncertainty rather than how sophisticated it is.

An ensemble carrying probabilities is by construction not a single-answer model, so the description contradicts the output it reports.

**B) The ice sheet's response is "nonlinear": a small additional warming past the threshold produces a loss far larger than the increment before it.**

A response is "nonlinear" when the output is not proportional to the input, so equal increments of forcing produce unequal effects. The colon supplies exactly that behaviour, with a small step past a threshold yielding a disproportionate loss. Thresholds are the most familiar source of nonlinearity in the cryosphere, which is why they dominate discussion of ice-sheet risk.

Effects that grow out of proportion to their cause is what the term names, so it describes this response accurately.

**C) The system shows "hysteresis", so the ice does not return at the same temperature at which it was lost.**

"Hysteresis" is present when a system's state depends on its history, so the return path differs from the outgoing one and thresholds are not symmetric. The sentence gives the standard test in a single clause: recovery requires conditions different from those under which the loss occurred. It is the reason some changes are described as effectively irreversible on human timescales.

A return path that does not retrace the outward one is hysteresis in the exact sense, so the term is correctly applied.

**D) Cloud behaviour is "parameterised", represented by a simplified rule because the processes are far smaller than the model's grid cells.**

To "parameterise" a process is to replace its explicit physics with a simplified relationship, which is necessary whenever the process is smaller than the model can resolve. The sentence names both the substitution and the reason for it, and the scale mismatch is the standard justification. Resolved processes are computed directly, which is the contrast the term implies.

A sub-grid process represented by a simplified rule is parameterised in the exact modelling sense, so the wording holds.

**E) The high-end scenario is "plausible" rather than likely, physically consistent but resting on assumptions few researchers expect to hold.**

"Plausible" says that something could happen without asserting that it probably will, which is why the sentence sets it against "likely" rather than against "impossible". The two clauses that follow supply the grounds on each side: physical consistency earns the plausibility, and doubted assumptions withhold the probability. The distinction is standard in risk assessment, where possible-but-improbable outcomes still matter.

Physical coherence without expected occurrence is exactly the space the word occupies, so it is well chosen here.

tasks.solution_overview: Historical writing about labour needs words for effort, environment, unwritten agreements, the fit between pay and risk, and disease that develops unnoticed. Each carries a register as well as a meaning, and the sentences here supply the concrete detail that earns it. Reading the evidence clause first shows how a formal word can be exactly right rather than merely elevated.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The work was "arduous": eight hours of hewing on the side, in a seam too low for a man to stand upright.**

"Arduous" describes work demanding sustained and severe physical effort, and it belongs to a formal register that suits historical narrative. The detail after the colon earns the adjective by specifying both the duration and the posture forced on the hewer. Difficult would be vaguer, since it says nothing about the bodily cost the word implies.

Hours of heavy labour in a seam that forbids standing is arduous in the fullest sense, so the description is apt.

**B) The barracks were "insalubrious", damp, unventilated, and shared in turn by men working three shifts around the clock.**

"Insalubrious" means unhealthy to live in, and the word is normally applied to housing, air or a district rather than to people. Damp, unventilated rooms occupied continuously by rotating shifts describes conditions unhealthy by every nineteenth-century measure. The formal register is doing real work here, since the term makes a claim about health rather than about comfort.

Accommodation that damages the health of those living in it is what the adjective names, so it fits these barracks.

**C) The agreement was "tacit", never written down and never announced, yet observed by both sides for thirty years.**

Something "tacit" is understood without being stated, so it is real in its effects while leaving no explicit record. The sentence gives both halves of that condition: nothing written or announced, and consistent observance over three decades. An agreement that was merely informal might still have been spoken aloud, which is the distinction the word preserves.

An understanding honoured for thirty years without ever being stated is tacit in the exact sense, so the term is right.

**D) Pay was not "commensurate" with the risk, a few pence above surface rates for work that killed one man in twenty.**

"Commensurate" means proportionate to something else, corresponding in scale, and it normally takes "with" before the thing compared. The sentence sets the two quantities side by side, a marginal premium against a mortality rate of one in twenty, so the reader can see the disproportion. The negation is what the evidence supports, since the comparison shows the two scales failing to match.

A few pence set against a death rate of that order is plainly out of proportion, so the denial of commensurability is well founded.

**E) Dust disease was "insidious", advancing without symptoms for decades before the first breathlessness appeared.**

"Insidious" describes harm that develops gradually and unnoticed, doing its damage before anything reveals it, and the medical use of the word keeps that sense exactly. Decades of silent progression followed by a late first symptom is the pattern the term was made for. Aggressive would describe speed instead, which is precisely what this disease did not have.

Long concealed progression that surfaces only when the damage is done is insidious in the strict sense, so the word fits.

tasks.solution_overview: These last items come from separate disciplines but reward the same reflex: take the word to its technical definition, then read the clause that reports the growth pattern, the price adjustment, the textual authority, the practical consequence or the status of the claim. One of them turns on how a proposition is held, assumed at the outset or earned through evidence, and that distinction decides the item. Where the surrounding detail belongs to the neighbouring term, that neighbour is the word the sentence needed.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The rise in recorded cases was called "exponential", adding the same fixed number of new patients every week for a year.**

"Exponential" growth multiplies by a constant factor in each period, so the absolute increase itself grows and doubling times can be quoted. A fixed number of new cases each week is a constant absolute increase, which is linear growth however large the weekly figure happens to be.

**Trap:** Exponential is borrowed constantly to mean merely fast; the test is whether the increase itself keeps growing, not whether the total is alarming.

The same increment every week describes a straight line rather than a curve, so the term misstates the shape of this rise.

**B) Wages had risen in "nominal" terms only, buying noticeably less at the end of the decade than at the beginning.**

A "nominal" figure is stated at the prices of the day, with no adjustment for inflation, which is why nominal growth can coexist with falling purchasing power. The sentence reports precisely that combination, since the number went up while what it bought went down. Real terms is the counterpart, and it is the adjusted measure that answers questions about living standards.

An unadjusted increase that leaves workers able to buy less is exactly what the qualifier warns of, so the wording is correct.

**C) The 1908 edition is "canonical", the text later scholars cite by default and against which variant readings are measured.**

A "canonical" text is the accepted standard version within a field, the one that other versions are compared against rather than merely one among many. The appositive supplies both marks of that status: default citation, and use as the reference point for variants. Definitive would claim finality, whereas canonical describes the position a text holds in scholarly practice.

Being the reference against which other readings are judged is what confers canonical status, so the term is used correctly.

**D) Whether the treaty still bound the island became "moot" once the state that had signed it ceased to exist.**

A question is "moot" when it no longer has any practical consequence, so that deciding it would settle nothing for anyone. The disappearance of the signatory state removes the party the obligation ran to, which is the standard way a live legal question becomes academic. The word says nothing about how interesting the question remains to historians.

A question with no remaining practical effect is moot in the established sense, so the sentence uses it properly.

**E) The claim was treated as "axiomatic", accepted only after three separate laboratories had confirmed it experimentally.**

Something "axiomatic" is taken as self-evident and assumed at the outset, which is exactly why axioms are not derived from evidence within the system that rests on them. A claim accepted only after three laboratories confirmed it has been established empirically, which is the opposite route to acceptance. Well-corroborated or firmly established is the description the evidence supports.

A proposition earned through repeated experiment is demonstrated rather than assumed, so the word misdescribes how this claim came to be accepted.
